one_liner: Rust CLI that pre-builds a disk-backed trigram index of a repo, then searches only candidate files, beating ripgrep in a first-party benchmark.
what_it_does: trigrep solves the same problem as grep/ripgrep (regex search over a code tree) but decouples indexing from querying: `trigrep index .` walks the repo once and writes a trigram inverted index under `.trigrep/`, then `trigrep search <pattern> .` decomposes the regex into literal fragments and only scans the resulting candidate files with a real regex engine. It is a separate CLI with its own flags, not a drop-in binary swap for grep/ripgrep, though default output is grep-compatible and `--json` mode exists for scripting.
how_it_is_fast: Indexing extracts every overlapping 3-byte trigram per file and writes a sorted, mmap'd lookup table (`lookup.bin`) plus posting lists (`postings.bin`), enabling binary search instead of a byte scan. At query time the regex is parsed into a `regex-syntax` HIR and decomposed into an AND/OR tree of literal trigrams; posting lists are intersected/unioned (smallest-first) to shrink the file set before the real regex engine ever runs. An 8-bit `loc_mask` (byte-offset adjacency) and an 8-bit `next_mask` Bloom filter on the following byte further prune false-positive candidates pre-verification. Indexing itself is parallelized with rayon.
when_to_use: Large, mostly-static trees (git.git-scale or bigger) searched repeatedly, so index-build cost amortizes
AI coding agents or scripted workflows issuing many regex searches per checkout, as the README targets
Patterns with real literal content (e.g. TODO|FIXME, ^#include) that decompose into selective trigrams
Need for grep-compatible text output or structured JSON output in the same tool
Prebuilt-binary install wanted on Linux/macOS (x86_64/aarch64) or Windows (x86_64) without a Rust toolchain
when_not_to_use: One-off or rarely-repeated searches on a tree: index-build time is excluded from the published benchmark and isn't amortized
Anything requiring code reuse or redistribution rights: no LICENSE file and no license field in either Cargo.toml, so it is reference-only
Patterns with no extractable literal (bare character classes, anchors, `.`) fall back to a MatchAll node, losing index selectivity
Decisions resting on the headline 1.58x: trigrep and ripgrep have the same 0.0500s median, so the gap is mean-only and close to the 10ms timer resolution used
Concurrent or long-lived multi-process use where index staleness/locking matters: thread/process safety around the on-disk index is not documented

integration.form: crate (trigrep-index library) + CLI binary (trigrep-cli), plus prebuilt release binaries
integration.dependencies: trigrep-cli: clap, regex, regex-syntax, anyhow, colored, rayon, atty. trigrep-index: memmap2, ignore, thiserror, serde, serde_json, rayon, byteorder
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2021 (workspace Cargo.toml), no MSRV stated
integration.platforms: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-apple-darwin, aarch64-apple-darwin, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (per release workflow targets)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — default output is grep-compatible and flags mirror grep/ripgrep conventions, but it requires an explicit `trigrep index .` step (or an implicit first-run build) before search, so it is not a binary drop-in replacement

gotchas: Search auto-builds the index if missing, so a cold first query pays full index-build cost that the published benchmark excludes
No LICENSE file and no license field in Cargo.toml: code can be read but not legally reused or redistributed
The next_mask adjacency filter is a Bloom filter (false positives possible, no false negatives); correctness depends on the final real-regex verification pass, not the index alone
`trigrep status` checks staleness against git HEAD but the index is not auto-refreshed on file edits without rerunning `trigrep index`
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick trigrep over ngi or ugrep-indexer mainly for its Cursor-derived on-disk format (mmap'd trigram lookup + loc/next-mask filtering) rather than for the strength of the evidence: ngi reports 1.7x-5.9x and ugrep-indexer 10x-21x with clearer separation, while trigrep's own numbers show tied medians and only a mean-based 1.58x over ripgrep.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README benchmark on a clone of git/git (4 patterns, 5 timed runs + 1 warmup each, index pre-built) reports mean query time 0.0405s for trigrep vs 0.0640s for ripgrep and 0.5990s for grep, i.e. ~1.58x and ~14.79x; medians for trigrep and ripgrep are tied at 0.0500s. Timed with `/usr/bin/time -p` (10ms resolution) over 20 samples; no CPU model or rustc version given, and index build time is excluded.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-04-30, 46 stars) but ships with no license, so usability is reference-only rather than reusable/redistributable.
